It shows the particle as once a noun: "the self of" the thing acted on. Hebrew's suffixed אֹתָם "themselves" (Jer 7:19; Ezk 34:2) keeps the same sense.

The derivation is uncertain: al-Azhari, as Lane gives him, says he heard none and suggests, "without being certain", the verb "aim at someone's person"; Wiktionary instead takes it from a vocative word. cognates.note: The noun of Hebrew אוֹת "sign". Its verb shows the sign of a person taken as the person's form or self, which is the bridge a derivation of the object marker from the root of אוֹת would need; Hebrew's suffixed אֹת־ has the same vowel as אוֹת. cognates.gloss: with; (Assyrian) from, with verbs of taking and receiving; with, in the possession of
cognates.note: Its uses match the Hebrew closely: "with" a person, "from" with verbs of taking (as מֵאֵת), and "with" of things in someone's keeping (as Gen 27:15). The older form išti makes the sound match with Hebrew ʾitt- less certain than the meaning.

doctrine.statement: "Yahweh was with Joseph" is shown in what followed: he prospered in all he did, even in prison, so that his master saw it (Gen 39:2–3, 21–23). Stephen retells it as "God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions" (Act 7:9–10). Caleb and Joshua give it as the reason not to fear the people of the land (Num 14:9); Yahweh promises it to Jeremiah as deliverance from those who fight him (Jer 1:8, 19), and through Haggai to the people rebuilding his house (Hag 1:13; 2:4). In scripture's use, then, Yahweh's being "with" someone is his help made visible in what happens to them, given to those he has called to a work, and it is the ground for not fearing.

Enoch "walked with God" (Gen 5:22, 24), and Noah, "a righteous man, blameless in his generations", "walked with God" (Gen 6:9): the walk is set beside righteousness and blamelessness. Malachi describes Levi's walk with Yahweh as true teaching in his mouth, no wrong on his lips, "in peace and uprightness he walked with me, and turned many from iniquity" (Mal 2:6). Hebrews reads Enoch's walk as pleasing God, and says that without faith it is not possible to please him (Heb 11:5–6). To walk with God, in scripture's use, is a whole life lived in his company, kept by faith and shown in uprightness.

Yahweh's covenants are made "with" named people and their seed: with Noah and his seed after him (Gen 9:9), with Abram, promising the land to his seed (Gen 15:18), and with Isaac, not Ishmael, "for an everlasting covenant for his seed after him" (Gen 17:19, 21). Through Isaiah he says of Israel, "this is my covenant with them" (Isa 59:21), and Paul applies the passage to Israel's future, when the deliverer comes out of Zion and their sins are taken away (Rom 11:26–27). The covenant is thus personal, made with Abraham and his seed, and still stands with Israel.

gloss: (object marker) the very one, untranslated; with suffixes me, him, them; (preposition) with, beside; (מֵאֵת) from
note: No Hebrew verb or noun is the source of either particle. (1) Object marker: Syriac ܝܬ (Payne Smith p. 198) is at once a noun "being, essence, self" and the accusative sign, and Jewish Aramaic יַת with a third-person suffix is "he himself" (Jastrow), so the particle was once a noun for the self of a thing; Hebrew's reflexive אֹתָם (Jer 7:19; Ezk 34:2, 8, 10) and its marking of subjects (Gen 21:5; 2Ki 6:5) fit that. A root behind the noun is not shown. The best lead is the root of אוֹת "sign": the suffixed form ʾōt- has the vowel of אוֹת, Phoenician ʾt is read /ʾot/ before suffixes, and Arabic files إِيَّا with آيَة "sign", whose verb is "aim at someone's آيَة, his form, person" (Lane pp. 131, 134); but al-Azhari's derivation is offered without certainty, Wiktionary gives a vocative origin for إِيَّا instead, and Hebrew אוֹת never means "self". A link to Aramaic אִיתַי "there is" (Jastrow's "v. אִית") is ruled out for Hebrew by the sounds: אִיתַי answers to Hebrew יֵשׁ with ṯ (Aramaic ת, Hebrew ש, as in Dan 3:12, which has both אִיתַי and יָתְהוֹן), while the particle has ת in Hebrew and Phoenician alike, an original t. (2) "With": suffixed ʾitt- (doubled t) against the marker's ʾōt-, so a different word; Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti/išti share its uses. Its relation to Akkadian ittu "sign" (eBL ittu II; the Akkadian cognate of אוֹת) is not supported: the preposition's older form is išti. No root found. Spellings: OSHB lemmas 853 (≈10,980) and 854 (≈890); BDB keys a.gm.aa and a.gn.aa share surface forms in the database, so counted uses overlap. Late books write 'with' as אוֹת־ (2Ki 1:15; 3:12; Jer 12:1; 35:2; Isa 59:21; Ezk 2:6), which OSHB often lemmatises as 853; read by sense. Left out: אַתְּ "you (f.)" (a.er.ad, from *ʾanti, for the entry of אַתָּה); the ploughshare אֵת, pl. אִתִּים (a.gq.ab, root אתת; 1Sa 13:20–21; Isa 2:4; Jol 4:10; Mic 4:3), probably a loan, for its own entry; Biblical Aramaic אָת "sign" (xa.ad.ab, Dan 3:32–33; 6:28), which the database files under את but which answers to Hebrew אוֹת and belongs in that entry. Names that may contain 'with' (אִתַּי Ittai, אִיתִיאֵל Ithiel) not written here. Greek: the object marker has no Greek word (the accusative case); Ecclesiastes' Septuagint renders it σύν, not aligned in MACULA, so not recorded. Open leads: Old Aramaic ʾyt (Sefire) in DEAPS; Ugaritic, which has no object marker, not consulted further; Ge'ez not consulted; CAD I/J itti not read (eBL used).
summary: Two particles share the spelling אֵת. The commoner is never translated: it points out the definite thing a verb acts on (אֶת־הָאָרֶץ; with suffixes אֹתִי "me", אֹתָם "them"), and sometimes the very thing a sentence is about even when that is the subject. The other, אִתִּי "with me" with suffixes, is "with": company, Yahweh's presence and help, dealings between two, nearness and keeping, and with מִן, "from beside". Neither grows from any verb or noun in scripture: the object marker was once a noun for a person's self, as its Syriac counterpart ܝܬ still is, and its suffixed forms can still mean "themselves" (Jer 7:19; Ezk 34:2). Whether that noun belongs to the root of אוֹת "sign" is not shown, and "with", which answers to Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti, has no known root.

words.gloss: (marks the definite object, untranslated); with suffixes me, you, him, them; the very…

senses.definition: Stands before the noun a verb acts on when that noun is definite: with the article, a name, or a possessive suffix. An object that is not definite goes without it, so the particle singles out a known, particular thing.

evidence.note: After אֶת נֹחַ, the words וְאֵת כָּל הַחַיָּה introduce all the wild animals as a second object of וַיִּזְכֹּר, “he remembered”.
God remembered Noah, all the wild animals, and all the livestock. Each object takes its own אֵת. In וְאֶת כָּל הַבְּהֵמָה the particle introduces the third object, “all the livestock.”
In אֶת שֵׁם אֶת חָם וְאֶת יָפֶת each son’s name has its own object marker. The final וְאֶת introduces Japheth as the third of the sons Noah fathered.
In אֶת שֵׁם אֶת חָם וְאֶת יָפֶת, each name is an object of וַיּוֹלֶד “he fathered”. The final וְאֶת introduces Japheth, the third son.
In וְאֵת הַכּוֹכָבִים ‘and the stars’, אֵת marks the stars as another direct object of וַיַּעַשׂ ‘made’, alongside the greater and lesser lights.
In וְאֶת הַבְּהֵמָה, the conjunction joins “the livestock” to the list of what God made. אֶת marks it as the second of three direct objects of וַיַּעַשׂ.
Yahweh God formed כָּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה וְאֵת כָּל עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “every animal of the field and every bird of the heavens.” Both phrases are objects of וַיִּצֶר. Only the second carries אֵת.
"He shall wave אֶת־הָעֹמֶר before Yahweh."
"Moses declared אֶת־מֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה to the sons of Israel."
"When you gather אֶת־תְּבוּאַת הָאָרֶץ you shall keep אֶת־חַג־יְהוָה seven days."
"When you reap אֶת־קְצִירָהּ … and bring אֶת־עֹמֶר רֵאשִׁית קְצִירְכֶם": the harvest and the sheaf of its firstfruits.
"Yahweh God formed אֶת־הָאָדָם, dust from the ground": the definite object takes the particle, the indefinite עָפָר does not.
"You shall love אֵת יְהוָה your God"; quoted in Mat 22:37, where the Greek marks the same noun by the accusative κύριον τὸν θεόν σου.

וְאֵת כָּל רֶמֶשׂ הָאֲדָמָה introduces the third object of וַיַּעַשׂ ‘he made’. Each of the three objects has its own marker.

senses.definition: Now and then before a noun with no article, where the thing is still a particular one in view.

senses.definition: Carries a pronoun suffix to make an object pronoun standing apart from the verb, often to put the person or thing first or to set it off.

evidence.note: Cain says גֵּרַשְׁתָּ אֹתִי, “you have driven me away.” The first-person suffix identifies Cain as the one driven away.
God blesses the seventh day and וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתוֹ, “he made it holy.” The masculine singular suffix refers back to יוֹם, “day,” as the object of the second verb.
In הַכּוֹת אֹתוֹ, ‘to strike him,’ אֹתוֹ refers to Cain. The following כָּל מֹצְאוֹ, ‘anyone who finds him,’ names the person who might strike him.
In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, “God blessed them,” אֹתָם refers back to the water creatures and birds of the preceding verse.
In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם, “and he blessed them,” אֹתָם refers to the male and female just named. The preceding בְּרָאָם, “he created them,” expresses the same object by a suffix on the verb.
In עָשָׂה אֹתוֹ, “he made him,” the suffix refers back to אָדָם, whom the preceding clause names as the one God created.

The verse shifts from בָּרָא אֹתוֹ, “he created him,” to זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם, “male and female he created them.” The plural suffix refers to the male and female together as the direct object of בָּרָא.
Yahweh tells Noah, אֹתְךָ רָאִיתִי צַדִּיק, “I have seen you to be righteous.” The suffixed particle places “you” before the verb and identifies Noah as the person seen.

"The appointed times of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim אֹתָם, them, holy convocations."

בְּהוֹצִיאִי אוֹתָם: "when I brought them out", spelled with ו.
הַצֹּרֵר אֶתְכֶם: "the adversary who oppresses you".
וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, “God blessed them.” אֹתָם identifies the people God blessed, the same people he then addresses.
כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים, “as God had commanded him.” The suffix on אֹתוֹ identifies Noah as the person God commanded.

senses.definition: The suffixed form can mean the person's own self, where English needs a reflexive: the particle points to the self of the one named.

"The shepherds fed אוֹתָם, themselves, and did not feed my flock."

senses.definition: Marks a noun that is not the verb's object: the subject of a passive or intransitive verb, or a noun set at the head of the sentence. Here it can only point out the thing itself, "this very one".

words.summary: About 11,000 times, the Hebrew Bible's commonest word after the conjunction. Unstressed it is joined by maqqef as אֶת־; with suffixes it is אֹת־ (אֹתוֹ, אֹתָם, also written אוֹת־), as Phoenician wrote ʾt /ʾot/ before a suffix and ʾyt elsewhere. It has no English word: it marks which noun the verb acts on, and the Greek marks the same noun by the accusative case. Its suffixed forms can mean "themselves" and it can mark a subject, so it is more than a case ending: it points to a thing's self. Syriac ܝܬ, the same word, is still a noun "being, self" as well as the accusative sign, which shows how the particle came to be; a root behind that noun is not shown.

evidence.note: "Noah knew אֵת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה לוֹ, what his youngest son had done to him."
"that Yahweh may bring upon Abraham אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר עָלָיו, what he has spoken of him".
"He commanded אֶת־אֲשֶׁר עַל־בֵּיתוֹ, the one who was over his house."

senses.definition: In company with someone: going, coming, being or walking together.

evidence.note: A covenant of salt before Yahweh with Aaron and his seed.
In וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתָּךְ, “I will establish my covenant with you,” אִתָּךְ identifies Noah as the person with whom God establishes the covenant.

words.summary: About 900 times. A separate word from the object marker, though spelled the same: with suffixes it is אִתִּי, אִתּוֹ, אִתָּנוּ, where the object marker is אֹתִי, אֹתוֹ. In some later books the suffixed forms are also written אוֹת־ (2Ki 1:15; Jer 12:1; Isa 59:21), so the two can only be told apart there by the sense. It alternates with עִם "with" in the same verse (Jdg 7:4; 2Sa 2:6), and its senses match Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti, even to "from" with verbs of taking; no verb or noun in scripture is its root.

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, once, with a suffix, where Hebrew would have אֹתָם. Elsewhere scripture's Aramaic marks the object with לְ. The Targums use it as Hebrew uses אֵת, and Syriac's ܝܬ, the same word, is also a noun "being, self".
